title: AI's Capability in Assisting Scientific Research in Physics, Astrophysics, and Cosmology I: Literature Review
authors: Hell, K. Vovk, Krishnaraj, Liu, Aizawa, Bayer, Blot, Cowell, Garg, Grée, Horowitz, Ichikawa, Iemoto, Kondo, Lorsin, McCarthy, Robinson, Ruiz-Granda, Thiele, I. Vovk & Zhou
tldr: On eight real physics projects, mid-2025 chatbots found useful papers the experts had missed but almost none of the experts' own picks, and 64% of their references had a wrong title, author, year or journal. ChatGPT Pro 5.5 got every reference right in a one-project test.

question.short: Can LLMs help physicists find the literature for a new research project?
question.detail: Researchers starting something new want a quick check of what has already been done. The authors ask whether chatbots can do this search at the research frontier, and how many of the papers they suggest an expert would actually use.

answer.short: As a helper, not a replacement: under 6% of the papers are shared with the expert's list, but the AI adds many relevant papers the expert missed.
answer.detail: Relevant papers found only by the AI make up 30–36% of each model's combined list with the expert's, against 36–53% found only by the expert. The AI searches by the project's keywords, while experts also reach for foundational work and neighbouring fields.

other_questions.short: How reliable are the references LLMs give?
other_questions.detail: Chatbots are known to invent citations. The authors check every AI reference the expert didn't also pick against the real paper.

answer.short: Mid-2025 models need checking: 3% of references don't exist and 64% have at least one wrong field. ChatGPT Deep Research is far better, and ChatGPT Pro 5.5 made no errors on one project.
answer.detail: Only 33% of the 641 references checked are fully correct. The first author is the field most often wrong. The authors think the newer models improve mainly because of their search and checking tools, not the language model alone.

why_important.headline: Too many papers to keep up with
why_important.detail: The number of new papers per day keeps growing, so important work is easy to miss, especially early in a project.

why_important.headline: Newcomers need a quick novelty check
why_important.detail: Someone entering a field first wants to know whether their idea has been done before committing to a full literature search.

why_important.headline: Researchers already use LLMs for this
why_important.detail: LLMs are increasingly used for literature reviews and paper feedback, but they are known to make up references.

why_important.headline: No direct test against experts at the frontier
why_important.detail: Comparisons of humans and AI on real research projects in physics are largely missing.

background.headline: Fake citations are a known problem
background.detail: Studies of 2023–2025 ChatGPT and Gemini models found many invented or garbled references across fields.

background.headline: AI in physics so far
background.detail: Machine learning already speeds up computations and parameter inference, e.g. lens modelling and the CAMELS simulations.

background.headline: LLMs as research partners
background.detail: LLMs are being tested on scientific tasks, reviewing and whole research projects.

background.headline: Part I of a series
background.detail: A companion paper (II) tests project planning and proposal evaluation.

setup.headline: Eight real frontier projects
setup.detail: Each was conceived by a graduate student or postdoc who works on the topic: AGN duty cycles, Lyman-break galaxies, intrinsic alignments, laser-machined anti-reflection structures, radio galaxies in HalfDome, the environment of gravitational-wave black holes, pulsar timing arrays and inflation from massive Yang–Mills fields (Table I).

setup.headline: Human and AI search in parallel
setup.detail: Each expert searched as usual and kept up to 50 important papers. Separately, AI prompters (students without experience in these projects) gave the same project to each model.

setup.headline: One standard prompt
setup.detail: A three-sentence background and a three-sentence goal written by the expert, asking for at most 50 refereed papers in four categories (reviews, highly cited, recent, other) as a table of title, first author, journal, year, DOI and link (Appendix B).

setup.headline: Three mid-2025 models, plus one 2026 model
setup.detail: ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research and Gemini 2.5 Flash, all with web search. ChatGPT Pro 5.5 (July 2026) was later run on the SU(2) project only.

setup.headline: The expert judges relevance
setup.detail: Each expert marked which AI suggestions were irrelevant to their project. The authors note this is subjective.

setup.headline: Matches need the same title and category
setup.detail: A paper the human called 'recent' and the AI called 'other' counts as two different papers, and one paper listed in two categories counts twice. This can make the overlap look smaller than it is.

setup.headline: Checking each AI reference
setup.detail: Every AI reference the expert didn't pick was looked up via its DOI, then its link, then its title, and compared with Crossref. Each ends up perfect, a metadata mismatch (real paper, at least one wrong field) or a fabrication (no such paper) (Fig. 1).

setup.headline: A controlled human-vs-AI test on real projects
setup.detail: The paper's new contribution is the design: the same frontier projects searched in parallel by their own experts and by LLMs, with the experts judging the AI's output.

method.headline: How much do the human and AI lists overlap?
method.detail: each model's references compared with the expert's, by category, over all eight projects (Fig. 2, Table II).

results.headline: Under 6% of papers are found by both
results.detail: Shared papers make up 4.3% (ChatGPT-4o), 5.4% (Deep Research) and 2.2% (Gemini) of each model's combined list with the expert's. None are shared in the 'other' category.

results.headline: The expert's papers are mostly missed
results.detail: Papers only the expert found are the largest group for every model: 45% (4o), 53% (Deep Research), 36% (Gemini).

results.headline: The AI adds many relevant papers
results.detail: Relevant papers only the AI found are 30% (4o), 36% (Deep Research) and 31% (Gemini), so the AI can fill gaps in an expert's search.

results.headline: Humans found 194 papers, the AI 701
results.detail: ChatGPT-4o gave 219, Deep Research 157 and Gemini 325 references over the eight projects.

method.headline: How many AI suggestions are relevant?
method.detail: the share of each model's combined list that the expert marked irrelevant (Table II).

results.headline: Only 6% irrelevant
results.detail: The fewest references, but nearly all on topic.

results.headline: 21% irrelevant
results.detail: 84 of its suggestions were marked irrelevant.

results.headline: 31% irrelevant
results.detail: Gemini gives the most references but also the most off-topic ones.

results.headline: Relevance is one person's opinion
results.detail: Each project had a single expert judge, and the authors note that relevance is subjective.

method.headline: What kinds of papers does each side pick?
method.detail: reading the titles chosen for each project, and the SU(2) project in detail.

results.headline: AI follows the keywords; experts go wider
results.detail: The AI picks papers matching the project's key words. Experts also choose foundational work and related fields.

results.headline: The expert reached into field theory
results.detail: The expert chose 14 foundational Yang–Mills papers; ChatGPT-4o and Pro 5.5 both stayed with inflation models, and neither picked papers far from cosmology.

results.headline: Based on reading titles, not measured
results.detail: This is the authors' impression from the titles, and they call the reason for the SU(2) difference speculation.

method.headline: Are the AI references real and correct?
method.detail: the 641 AI references the expert didn't pick (each paper counted once), checked against Crossref (Fig. 1, Table III).

results.headline: Only a third are fully correct
results.detail: 211 (33%) are perfect, 408 (64%) are real papers with at least one wrong field, and 22 (3%) don't exist.

results.headline: A partly wrong field also counts as wrong
results.detail: Fields that disagree only partly are counted as mismatches, so some of the 64% may be small errors.

results.headline: Only the AI-only references were checked
results.detail: References that the expert also picked aren't checked.

method.headline: Which model is most reliable?
method.detail: the same check split by model (Table III, Fig. 3).

results.headline: No fabrications, 78% perfect
results.detail: 108 of 139 perfect, 31 (22%) mismatched. The authors credit its stronger search and checking tools.

results.headline: 1 fabrication, but 76% mismatched
results.detail: 149 of 196 references have a wrong field.

results.headline: Most fabrications
results.detail: 21 of 306 references (7%) don't exist and 228 (75%) are mismatched.

results.headline: Gemini was the fast default model
results.detail: The study used Gemini 2.5 Flash, the default in mid-2025, not Google's larger Pro model.

method.headline: Which details are wrong?
method.detail: the 399 mismatches whose real paper could be found from a working DOI or link (Table IV).

results.headline: First author is wrong most often
results.detail: First author 306, title 181, journal 124, year 105. Most often two of the four fields are wrong (206 papers).

results.headline: 9 more have a broken DOI and link
results.detail: They were found only by title, so their fields couldn't be checked.

method.headline: Have newer models improved?
method.detail: ChatGPT Pro 5.5 (July 2026) run on the SU(2) project with the same prompt, against ChatGPT-4o (Sec. III C, Fig. 3).

results.headline: Every reference correct
results.detail: 44 papers, 4 shared with the expert; all 40 checked were perfect, with no fabrications.

results.headline: Still little overlap with the expert
results.detail: Each model shares 4 papers with the expert's 14, and the two models share 7 papers with each other.

results.headline: One project only
results.detail: Pro 5.5 was tested on a single project, so its perfect score is a spot check, not a benchmark.

conclusion.headline: Use AI and human searches together
conclusion.detail: Experts and LLMs each find many relevant papers the other misses, so combining them gives a fuller reading list.

conclusion.headline: Check every mid-2025 AI reference
conclusion.detail: 3% are fabricated and 64% have a wrong field. Deep Research did much better, with no fabrications.

conclusion.headline: The improvement probably comes from the tools
conclusion.detail: Deep Research's and Pro 5.5's accuracy likely reflects web search, checking and more computing time, not the language model alone.

conclusion.headline: AI searches more narrowly
conclusion.detail: It follows the project's keywords; experts also bring in foundations and neighbouring fields.

conclusion.headline: Caveat: eight projects, one expert each
conclusion.detail: A larger study with more projects is needed.

conclusion.headline: Caveat: the 2026 test is one project
conclusion.detail: The Pro 5.5 result needs a systematic benchmark before it can be trusted.

figures.caption: How each AI reference was checked: DOI first, then the link, then a title search. Each ends up perfect, a metadata mismatch or a fabrication.
For each model and paper type: papers found by both (green), only by the expert (pink), only by the AI and relevant (blue), and by the AI but irrelevant (grey).
Per model: AI references that are perfect (green), mismatched (yellow) or fabricated (red). Pro 5.5 is for the SU(2) project only.

glossary.meaning: Digital Object Identifier: a permanent ID for a published paper that resolves to its web page.
The registry of DOIs, which holds each paper's official title, authors, year and journal.
